opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, because when I started in deep RL, around the time of DQN and AlphaGo, there was a sense that we had cracked something fundamental. We had a general-purpose learning algorithm that could go from pixels to superhuman play. A decade later, if you ask how many real-world systems run on deep RL as the core technology, the answer is surprisingly few, with the big exception of RL from human feedback in language models, which is a rather special case.

I think there are a few interlocking reasons.

The first is that our methods are incredibly brittle. If you take a standard algorithm like PPO and change the random seed, a hyperparameter, or some implementation detail that isn't even in the paper, you can get wildly different results. In the real world you can't run a thousand seeds and report the best one. You need something that works the first time, or at least reliably, and we've never really delivered that.

The second is a methodological problem in how we do research. For a long time the field optimized for a handful of benchmarks: Atari, MuJoCo, a few others. We got very good at squeezing performance out of those, but often in ways that don't transfer. Part of the reason was computational. Running enough experiments to make statistically meaningful claims was so expensive that people ran three seeds and called it a day. That's one reason we've invested heavily in things like JAX-based end-to-end training on accelerators. If you can run thousands of agents in parallel in minutes instead of days, you can do science properly, with real hyperparameter sweeps, many seeds, and proper ablations. A lot of what looked like algorithmic progress turns out to be noise once you do that.

The third, and maybe the deepest, is generalization. Deep RL agents tend to overfit massively to the exact environment they're trained in. The real world is never the training environment. It's always shifted, always a bit different. So you need agents that are robust across a distribution of environments, and ideally ones that learn to adapt. That pushes you towards meta-learning, unsupervised environment design, and open-ended training, where the curriculum itself is generated, rather than hand-crafting one task and hoping.

And then there's the multi-agent aspect, which is close to my heart. Most real-world settings involve other agents: humans, other AI systems, institutions. Standard RL treats everything else as a stationary environment, which is simply false. If you deploy an agent that has only learned to coordinate with copies of itself, it can fail completely with a human partner. That's the motivation behind things like zero-shot coordination.

So it's not that RL as a framework is wrong. Decision-making under uncertainty is exactly the problem we care about. But the specific recipe of taking a single simulator, a single reward function, and a brittle algorithm and turning the crank hasn't produced robust, general, deployable agents. The exciting part now is that foundation models give us priors we never had before. Combine those with RL done carefully, at scale and with proper science, and I think we may finally start seeing the real-world impact people hoped for ten years ago.

r001.rationale: The response attributes limited impact to brittleness, benchmark overfitting, weak generalization, and multi-agent challenges, but does not present unfavorable hardware fit as a hypothesis.

r002.rationale: It mentions costly experiments and parallel training on accelerators, but does not identify CPU-run environments paired with GPU-run agents as the cause.

r003.rationale: It describes JAX-based training on accelerators, but does not state that running both environments and agents on GPUs turns hardware fit into an advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that deep RL has been optimized, as a field, for a very particular kind of problem that doesn't look much like the real world. We got extremely good at taking a simulator, say Atari or MuJoCo or Go, and finding a policy that exploits that exact simulator. And the agents that come out of that are, in a sense, overfit to the environment they were trained in. The moment you change something, even slightly, they break.

The real world isn't like that. In the real world you almost never get the same environment at test time that you had at training time. There are other agents whose behavior you don't control, there's distribution shift, there's partial observability, and crucially there's a human in the loop who has to actually trust and use the thing. So we've been measuring progress along an axis that was convenient for benchmarks rather than one that reflects what deployment actually requires.

The second issue, which I think is underappreciated, is sample efficiency and the cost of the whole pipeline. Deep RL works when you can run millions or billions of environment interactions cheaply. In most real domains you can't. You can't crash the robot a million times, and you can't run a million A/B tests on a hospital. So either you build a simulator, in which case you're back to the sim-to-real gap problem, or you work from offline data, which brings its own set of difficulties around coverage and extrapolation.

And then there's a cultural point. For a long time the field had a bit of an "end-to-end or nothing" mindset. Everything had to be learned from scratch from reward. That's an elegant research framing, but practitioners have decades of structure, priors, and domain knowledge that we often threw away. The places where RL has genuinely had impact, like RLHF for language models or some of the data center cooling work, are exactly the places where it's been used as a component inside a larger system with a lot of structure already in place, rather than as the whole solution.

So I don't think the ideas were wrong. I think we spent a lot of effort climbing the wrong hill, and the interesting work now is in things like generalization across environments, multi-agent and open-ended settings, and building agents that are robust to being wrong about the world, because they always will be.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the problem is that we’ve often focused on settings where the hardest practical problems have already been solved for us. You have a simulator, you have a reward function, you can collect enormous amounts of experience, and you have a fairly clear way of measuring progress. Under those conditions, deep reinforcement learning can do remarkable things.

But in a real application, those conditions are usually what you’re missing. Where does the experience come from? Can you afford to explore? Does the reward actually capture what you want? And if you train in simulation, does the policy still work when you deploy it?

There’s also a question of whether you need reinforcement learning in the first place. If you can solve a problem with supervised learning, or with a good controller, that’s often a much simpler engineering proposition. RL needs to provide enough additional value to justify the complexity and the cost of collecting data.

So I wouldn’t say the underlying idea has failed. I’d say that getting better at a benchmark and making a method useful are different objectives, and we haven’t always been sufficiently explicit about that distinction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulators, data, and deployment, but does not propose unfavorable hardware fit as a reason for RL's limited impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the problem is that we’ve been very focused on benchmarks where you can generate essentially unlimited experience. You have a simulator, you have a reward function, and you can run the thing for billions of steps. That’s a very particular setting. In the real world, collecting experience is expensive, the reward is often difficult to specify, and exploration can have consequences.

And there’s a bit of a chicken-and-egg problem. If you want to apply reinforcement learning to a real system, you need the infrastructure to collect data, deploy policies, and evaluate them reliably. That can be a much bigger investment than developing the algorithm itself. Often, a simpler approach will already solve enough of the problem that it’s hard to justify that investment.

So I wouldn’t necessarily say that the underlying idea has failed. I think we’ve underestimated the gap between getting an agent to perform well in a carefully defined environment and building a system that is useful under real-world constraints. Better benchmark performance doesn’t automatically close that gap.
